newsitem.title: BRAZIL: USDA Brazil soybean crop forecast is low - analysts.
newsitem.headline: USDA Brazil soybean crop forecast is low - analysts.

text.p: A U.S. agricultural attache's forecast that Brazil's soybean crop will be 26 million tonnes in 1996/97 was on the low side and the crop may be closer to 27 million tonnes, Brazilian analysts and traders said.
"It's a conservative forecast," said Dr Carlos Cogo, analyst at Agromercados.

He predicted that the crop would be a record 26.5 to 27 million tonnes instead, saying that climate conditions were still favourable despite the low level of rains in some areas of the key producing state of Rio Grande do Sul.
The attache, posted at the U.S. embassy in Sao Paulo, based his forecast on 12 million hectares planted. It matches the official USDA forecast released on December 12th.
Paulo Molinari, analyst at independent consultants Safras e Mercado, said he expected the Brazilian 1996/97 crop to come in between 26 and 27 million tonnes.
"It will depend on the climate conditions in the next 60 days which is the flowering and pod formation phase," he said.
The most recent Safras estimate was for a 1996/97 crop of 26.28 million tonnes, based on a total planted area of 11.36 million hectares.
This was down 0.4 percent on its earlier forecast, mainly due to severe credit problems which had resulted in a smaller planted area than originally predicted.
But it was still above the previous record crop of 25.9 million tonnes in 1994/95.

Molinari said lack of rains were mainly affecting the south and south-east of Rio Grande do Sul but in the north and north-east of the state, where most of its soybeans were planted, rainfall was normal.
"In the areas where there is dryness there is very little soybean planted," he said.
The lack of rainfall would only become a problem if it continued through the flowering period, expected to begin in late January, the analyst added.
Cooperatives said they expected generalized rainfall in Rio Grande do Sul and Parana states overnight, which would help to replenish soil moisture in areas starved of water.

Independent meteorologist Somar earlier this week predicted that rainfall would remain moderate until January 13 to 14 but cold fronts would move into the south next week bringing with them more widespread rains.
Analysts said that apart from the weather, one factor which could dampen this year's crop forecasts was the low use of fertilisers by cash-strapped farmers.
But even that was not a big concern, according to Cogo at Agromercados. "The climate has ended up compensating for the low use of fertilisers," he said.

One trader said he was not excessively worried about the drop in fertiliser use and he expected the crop to come in between 26.3 and 26.8 milion tonnes. But he added it was unlikely to exceed 27 million tonnes.
"I would be very surprised," the trader said.
